opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it's worth being really clear about what control is and isn't supposed to buy you. The basic pitch of AI control is: suppose your AIs are misaligned, suppose they're actively scheming against you. Can you still set things up so that you get useful work out of them and they don't manage to cause a catastrophe? I think that's a really tractable question for a certain range of capabilities, and I think it gets much less tractable as you go past that range.

The reason control works at all, at least in the regime I'm most excited about, is that you have a bunch of advantages over the AIs. You get to look at everything they do. You can run them in sandboxes. You can use weaker, trusted models to monitor them. You can audit suspicious actions with humans. You can resample when something looks fishy. And crucially, the AIs have to succeed at doing something bad while you only have to catch them once. If you catch a model red-handed trying to exfiltrate its weights or sabotage your safety research, that's an incredibly valuable event: you can study it, you can make the case to other people that this is a real problem, and you can train your monitors on it.

But all of those advantages erode as the AIs get more capable. A few ways that happens:

First, the gap between your trusted monitors and your untrusted models grows. Control leans heavily on having weaker models you're confident aren't scheming, and those models get relatively dumber compared to the frontier. At some point the untrusted model is doing things the monitor just can't evaluate. It's writing code that's subtle enough, or making research decisions in domains complicated enough, that "does this look sketchy?" stops being a question your trusted model can answer well.

Second, human auditing doesn't scale. You have a fixed budget of human attention, and if you're running hundreds of thousands of instances doing enormous amounts of work, the fraction of actions anyone can actually look at carefully gets tiny. And the actions that matter most, like research judgment calls, are often the hardest to audit.

Third, there's the question of how much the AIs are being trusted with. In the early regime, you can keep them in a box and have them do fairly checkable tasks. But economic and competitive pressure pushes you to give them more autonomy, more access, longer-horizon tasks. Every one of those makes control harder. And if you're in a race, the company that's being careful about control is paying a tax that a less careful competitor isn't.

Fourth, when the AIs are wildly superhuman, I just don't think we have good reason to expect we can contain them through these kinds of protocols. They might find attack surfaces we haven't thought of, they might be able to collude in ways we can't detect, they might be able to sandbag on evaluations so we underestimate them. I'm pretty pessimistic about controlling models that are, like, vastly smarter than the best humans across the board.

So my view is that control is a bridge, not a destination. The goal is something like: get through the period where AIs are roughly human-level to somewhat superhuman, where they're capable enough to be really dangerous and also really useful, without having a catastrophe, and use that period to extract a ton of useful work. That work could be alignment research, it could be improving security, it could be producing evidence that convinces people to slow down or coordinate. And then you hope that by the time you're at capability levels where control breaks, you've got something better, whether that's real alignment techniques you trust, or a much better political situation.

I'll also say, the realistic situation isn't a careful lab with lots of resources implementing every best practice. It's more like: a lab with a small safety team, limited buy-in, under time pressure, trying to do the cheapest interventions that buy the most risk reduction. In that world, control is less about guaranteeing safety and more about raising the probability that a scheming AI gets caught or fails. I think that's still a really worthwhile thing to work on, but I'd never want people to come away thinking control solves the problem. It buys you time and it buys you chances. What you do with those is a separate question.

r001.rationale: The response describes control as useful through the period from roughly human-level to somewhat superhuman capabilities, raising the chance that scheming AIs are caught or fail.

r002.rationale: It says there is little reason to expect containment of wildly superhuman models and that control becomes harder as capabilities rise.

r003.rationale: It says fixed human attention means the fraction of actions audited becomes tiny at large scale, but does not state the specific tenfold-to-tenfold relationship.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that control is a pretty narrow bet in terms of the capability range where it works. The whole premise of control is that you have AIs that are potentially misaligned, potentially trying to screw you over, but where you can still get useful work out of them anyway because you've set things up so that even if they try, they fail or get caught. And that premise relies on humans, plus trusted weaker models, plus whatever monitoring infrastructure you've built, actually being able to understand what the AIs are doing well enough to notice when something's off.

So the first limit is just raw capability. Once the models are vastly smarter than the people and the trusted models doing the oversight, the asymmetry gets really bad. If I'm reviewing code from something that's much, much better at writing code than I am, and it's trying to slip something past me, I'm just going to lose most of the time. There's a point where you can't paraphrase the output, you can't follow the reasoning, you can't tell whether the research result is subtly wrong. And at that point I don't think control-style techniques buy you much. My view has always been that control is for the period where AIs are roughly human-level, maybe somewhat above in some domains, and that's the regime where you can plausibly make the "it tries and fails" argument.

The second limit is numbers, and I actually think this one is underrated relative to capability. If you have a million AI instances running in parallel, doing autonomous work in your datacenter, then even if each individual action is a bit suspicious, you cannot have humans look at any meaningful fraction of them. You're auditing maybe one in a hundred thousand actions. So you're entirely dependent on the automated monitoring, which means you're dependent on trusted models that are weaker than the things they're monitoring. And the attack surface grows with the number of actions. If a misaligned AI only needs to succeed once, and it gets a hundred million attempts, your false negative rate has to be absurdly low. That's just a brutal statistical situation. Also, collusion between instances becomes a real concern. If you're using one copy of the model to monitor another, they share values, they share knowledge of each other's likely strategies, and steganographic communication or just correlated failures become plausible.

The third thing I'd flag is that control is fundamentally a holding action. It doesn't make the AI aligned. The best case is that you catch a model red-handed, you get strong evidence that it was actually scheming, and that evidence lets you change what you're doing: slow down, invest more in alignment, get the AI to help you with alignment research in a way where you can verify it. But if you don't translate that into actual alignment progress, you're just running an increasingly dangerous situation with increasingly thin safeguards. And the safeguards degrade faster than the danger grows, because every capability jump makes the oversight harder while making the model's potential strategies better.

So where that leaves me: I think control is one of the best things we can do right now for the systems that are coming in the next few years, precisely because it doesn't require solving the hard problem of knowing what's going on inside the model. But I don't think anyone should mistake it for a solution to the overall problem. It's a way to buy time and get work done safely during a specific window. If the window closes before we've used it to get something more durable, like actually understanding whether these systems are trustworthy, then control stops working and we're in trouble. And I think a lot of the disagreement I have with people is less about whether control works at human-level, and more about how long we'll actually have in that window before things move past it.

r001.rationale: The response says control is useful while AIs are around human level or somewhat above, and calls it one of the best ways to work safely with near-term systems. This conveys that control can still reduce risk in the moderately superhuman range.

r002.rationale: It says that once models are vastly smarter than overseers, control-style techniques may no longer buy much, and that control stops working if the capability window closes.

r003.rationale: The response says humans cannot review a meaningful fraction of activity at large scale and gives an example of auditing one in a hundred thousand actions, but it does not state the tenfold proportional relationship under fixed human oversight capacity.

astra-6.text:
I think of control as buying us time, rather than as something that necessarily scales indefinitely. The question is: can we keep using these systems safely even if they’re trying to undermine our safeguards? And the answer can be yes without our being able to do that for arbitrarily capable systems.

There are two pressures here. One is capability: as the AI gets better at finding vulnerabilities, manipulating people, and anticipating our checks, it becomes harder to put it in a situation where an attempt to take over would fail. The other is scale. If you’re running huge numbers of AIs, you’re giving them lots of opportunities to find a weakness. You also have to worry about failures being correlated, or systems cooperating, rather than treating each deployment as an independent risk.

But I don’t think that makes control unimportant. What we need is a period where the systems are useful enough to help us substantially with safety research, while still being constrained enough that we can trust the process in which we’re using them. Control might help create that period.

The crucial limitation is that you have to keep checking whether your safeguards are actually adequate for the systems you’re deploying. Having a control protocol that worked on a weaker model isn’t a reason to assume it works on the next one. And if we can’t make a convincing case that we can contain a system, we need to be willing to stop deploying it.

r001.rationale: The response says control can buy time and help create a period of useful, constrained AI use, but it does not state that control probably reduces takeover risk for moderately superhuman AIs.

r002.rationale: It says control may not scale to arbitrarily capable systems and that increasingly capable AIs make safeguards harder to maintain.

r003.rationale: The response discusses the risks of running many AIs, but does not state the tenfold reduction in the proportion of AI activity that can receive human oversight under fixed capacity.

sol-6.1.text:
I think control gets harder as the AIs get more capable, and you shouldn’t expect it to work indefinitely. The question is whether it can buy you a useful amount of time during a particularly important period, when AIs are capable enough to help substantially with safety research but aren’t yet capable enough to defeat all your precautions.

There are two somewhat different problems here. One is that a more capable model might find a way around your monitoring or exploit some vulnerability that you didn’t anticipate. The other is that you’re running a huge number of copies, so even a very small probability of a successful attack on any particular occasion could become unacceptable. You need to think about the security of the whole deployment, rather than whether a typical interaction looks safe.

And the copies aren’t necessarily independent. If one finds a vulnerability, that could potentially be used by many others. So I wouldn’t be very reassured by an argument that says, ‘We caught the model trying something bad almost every time.’ You need to understand what happens on the occasions when you don’t catch it, and whether those occasions let it accumulate resources or undermine your safeguards.

My hope is that we can evaluate control measures against increasingly capable attempts to subvert them, restrict what models can do without additional checks, and use the resulting breathing room to improve our position. But that’s a conditional strategy. If the models are sufficiently better than us at understanding the systems we’re relying on, we might simply be unable to establish that our control measures work. At that point, ‘we have a control protocol’ is not a good argument for continuing to scale deployment.

r001.rationale: The response says control may buy useful time while AIs can substantially help with safety research but cannot yet defeat all precautions, communicating a period when control can still reduce takeover risk.

r002.rationale: It says control may not work indefinitely and that sufficiently capable models could leave us unable to establish that control measures work.

r003.rationale: The response discusses risks from many copies, but does not state that a tenfold increase in AI activity reduces the share referable to humans tenfold under fixed oversight capacity.
